A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PrivAct research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, figures and tables can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original PrivacyLens and ConfAIde evaluations, component ablations, topology experiments and a qualitative case study, including supplementary results.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds GPT-4o judging, hyperparameter sensitivity results and compositional-privacy evaluation in Appendix D.3-D.5.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same multi-agent generation, reward propagation, preference construction, DPO training and LC-ARS reward. Appendix D.5 evaluates previously trained verifier/refiner models in another defense framework without introducing a new training algorithm or method component.

E1.justification: Appendix D.5 adds a compositional-privacy dataset with 119 scenarios evaluated under benign and adversarial conditions. Recovering sensitive information by combining individually innocuous responses substantially extends the evaluated threat scenarios beyond the retained PrivacyLens and ConfAIde tasks.

E2.justification: Table 9 introduces a Chain-of-Thought defense comparator for the new compositional-privacy evaluation. Vanilla LM, PPE and AIFC remain the comparators in the corresponding PrivacyLens comparisons; the original ConfAIde and topology comparator sets are unchanged.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce GPT-4o evaluation of the same outputs, additional reward-parameter configurations, and a paired benign/adversarial Overall Success protocol using a Llama-3.1-8B defender and Qwen3-32B attacker. Existing PrivacyLens splits, training settings and K=10 response sampling remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix D.3 adds a cross-judge robustness check. D.4 adds six alpha/beta configurations and expands the reported b2 settings from three to nine, substantially extending sensitivity analysis. The component ablations in Figures 3 and 5, topology tests and case study already appeared in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions retain K=10 response samples per test case, without adding training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. D.3 newly quotes human-agreement statistics from Shao et al. (2024); these are prior-work validation results, not a new statistical estimation procedure for PrivAct.

E6.justification: Tables 6-9 add alternative-judge scores, sensitivity outcomes and compositional-privacy results, including 42.39% Overall Success for CoT versus 46.34% with the b2=0.3 refiner. Table 5 also rescales average helpfulness from 0-3 to the documented 0-1 scale; these conversions represent unchanged outcomes, not performance gains.

T1.justification: The problem formulation, preference construction and LC-ARS equation are unchanged, with no added proofs or formal propositions. The new benchmark's inherited Overall Success metric and empirical parameter sweeps do not revise the mathematical framework.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about internalizing contextual privacy, improving privacy-helpfulness tradeoffs and generalizing across tasks and agent topologies. The stated maximum leakage reduction remains 12.32%.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning cross-judge consistency, parameter sensitivity and b2-controlled privacy-helpfulness tradeoffs. The Impact Statement newly identifies limited direct applicability to closed-source models because fine-tuning is required. These are focused extensions of the existing interpretations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: The new appendix studies specify the additional judge, tested parameter configurations, attacker/defender models and deployment of trained verifier/refiner models. Existing prompts, training commands, batching, epochs, preference-dataset sizes and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds He et al. (2026) and Kim et al. (2026), and expands discussion of the already cited Patil et al. (2025) into an evaluated compositional-privacy setting. The ConfAIde reference update identifies the same work, while the principal novelty positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Changes include localized metric explanations and attribution edits, reordered acknowledgements and Impact Statement, an expanded appendix outline, named D.1-D.5 subsections and a new Limitations section. The main narrative and method exposition are largely retained.

P2.justification: Four substantive tables are added for alternative judging, parameter sensitivity and compositional privacy. Table 5 is resized and the supplementary material is reorganized around subsection headings and wrapped tables. Figures 1-5 retain identical image content, and the original main-table structures remain intact.

improvement.justification: The added judge check, sensitivity studies and compositional-privacy evaluation provide useful scrutiny beyond v1, while Table 5's normalization correction improves consistency. The gain is limited by overly broad judge-consistency language: the same Mistral-7B PrivAct outputs at b2=0.3 receive average helpfulness of 0.863 versus 0.472 under different judges. Overall, the supplementary evidence and clearer applicability limits improve the paper without fully resolving evaluation reliability.
